pos: n. (the father of one of Solomon's twelve commissariat officers, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Deqer, probably a stab or a thrust, from a root meaning to pierce; named once in Scripture, at 1 Kings 4:9, where the Authorized Version margin offers “Ben Dekar” for “the son of Dekar.”
biblical_def: Dekar is named once, and not for anything he did: “The son of Dekar, in Makaz, and in Shaalbim, and Bethshemesh, and Elonbethhanan” (1 Kings 4:9). We are given the father's name and not the son's, which is how several of Solomon's twelve officers appear in that register; the Authorized Version notes in the margin that the phrase may be read as the proper name Ben Dekar. These twelve were the backbone of the kingdom's administration, each responsible for a month's provision for a vast household: “And those officers provided victual for king Solomon, and for all that came unto king Solomon's table, every man in his month: they lacked nothing” (1 Kings 4:27). The chapter is careful about them. It names the chief of them — “And Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers: and Zabud the son of Nathan was principal officer, and the king's friend” (1 Kings 4:5) — and it even records the fodder: “Barley also and straw for the horses and dromedaries brought they unto the place where the officers were, every man according to his charge” (1 Kings 4:28). A man remembered only as somebody's father, in a list of quartermasters, is in the Word of God forever.

corruption_summary: Administrative faithfulness is counted spiritually negligible, when Scripture records the quartermasters of Solomon by name and even itemises their fodder.
corruption_paragraphs: No sermon has ever been preached on Dekar, and 1 Kings 4 is skipped in most reading plans. Yet the Holy Ghost names these men and records that under their hands the king's house lacked nothing. Ordinary competence exercised in a lawful office is a species of faithfulness, and a church that only honours the visible and the eloquent has a narrower register of honour than the Bible does.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God records what the competent did as well as what the eloquent said, and that a man known to Scripture only as another man's father is known to Scripture.

pos: n. (the father of Shelemiah, one of the three officers sent to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Abdi'el, servant of God, from 'ebed, a servant, and 'El, God; named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 36:26.
biblical_def: Abdeel's name means servant of God, and it appears once, attached to a son employed in the opposite business: “But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them” (Jeremiah 36:26). The occasion is one of the boldest acts of contempt for the word of God in the Old Testament. Jehoiakim had the prophecy read to him and destroyed it column by column as it came: “And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth” (Jeremiah 36:23). Then he sent three men, one of them the son of a man named Servant-of-God, to arrest the prophet and his scribe. The chapter's answer to the penknife is final: “Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, after that the king had burned the roll” (Jeremiah 36:27), and the roll was rewritten with additions: “and there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jeremiah 36:32). A king can burn a copy. He cannot burn the Word.

corruption_summary: Attacks on the Bible are imagined to be modern and intellectual, when Jeremiah 36 shows the oldest and commonest form of them: destroy the copy and silence the reader.
corruption_paragraphs: Jehoiakim did not refute Jeremiah. He cut the scroll with a penknife and sent constables after the men who wrote it. That remains the preferred method where argument is inconvenient — suppress the text, discredit or detain the messenger. The chapter's reply is the doctrine of providential preservation in narrative form: the roll was rewritten, longer than before, and the king who burned it has his sentence recorded in the book he destroyed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Word of God is indestructible while its copies are not, and that the LORD hid Baruch and Jeremiah because He intended the book to be finished.

pos: n. (a Reubenite captain among David's valiant men, named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Adina', slender or delicate, from a root meaning to be soft or luxurious; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 11:42.
biblical_def: Adina is named once, in the Chronicler's roll of David's valiant men: “Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him” (1 Chronicles 11:42). The name means slender or delicate, which is a quiet irony in a list of warriors; what he was called and what he was are two things. Two details in the verse are worth noting. First, he is a Reubenite, from the tribe east of Jordan which Deborah had once rebuked for staying home. David's army drew from the whole nation, and the men who came to him in the wilderness came out of tribes with poor records. Second, he brought thirty men with him. He is not merely a name on a muster but a captain with a company, and the Chronicler notes the company. The list around him is a list of the unsung: “Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai” (1 Chronicles 11:41) immediately before him, and after the famous names — “Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 11:26) — the roll runs on to its last and least-known entries: “Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite” (1 Chronicles 11:47).

corruption_summary: Lists of names are passed over as dead weight, when the Chronicler's muster roll is a deliberate act of remembering men the world forgot.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 11 ends in a long tail of names nobody recognises, and that tail is the point. The Chronicler had the famous three and the famous thirty to write about and he kept writing, down to Jasiel the Mesobaite. God's memory does not thin out at the bottom of the list. A man who commanded thirty Reubenites and is named once will be named at the resurrection too.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that David's strength was made of captains no one remembers, and that the Lord records the company a man brought as well as the name he bore.

pos: n. (one of Solomon's twelve commissariat officers, set over Mahanaim)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achinadab, my brother is noble or willing, from 'ach, a brother, and nadab, to be willing or to offer freely; named once in Scripture, at 1 Kings 4:14.
biblical_def: Ahinadab is named once, in a verse of four words of substance: “Ahinadab the son of Iddo had Mahanaim” (1 Kings 4:14). His name means my brother is noble, or my brother is willing, from the root that gives the freewill offering its name. He was one of the twelve officers over the districts of Israel, and his district was Mahanaim east of Jordan — the place where Jacob met the angels and where Abner had fled in the night. The register he stands in records the system plainly: “And those officers provided victual for king Solomon, and for all that came unto king Solomon's table, every man in his month: they lacked nothing” (1 Kings 4:27). One of his fellow-officers is singled out for the hardest post: “Geber the son of Uri was in the country of Gilead, in the country of Sihon king of the Amorites, and of Og king of Bashan; and he was the only officer which was in the land” (1 Kings 4:19). And the chapter even accounts for the animals: “Barley also and straw for the horses and dromedaries brought they unto the place where the officers were” (1 Kings 4:28). A willing brother is what the kingdom needed, and what his name said he was.

corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew root behind Ahinadab is the one that gives Israel the freewill offering — the gift nobody compelled. A kingdom runs on such men, and the Bible is content to name them once and move on, which is itself a lesson for anyone who serves in a post that will never be noticed. The record exists; it is simply not in the hands of the people the servant works among.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that willing service rendered in an unseen office is service God names, and that the honour of such work does not depend on being remembered by men.

pos: n. (a descendant of Shobal in the line of Judah, head of the Zorathite families)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achumay, of uncertain meaning, perhaps brother of water or brother of the Umaites; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 4:2.
biblical_def: Ahumai is named once, three generations down a short line in the register of Judah: “And Reaiah the son of Shobal begat Jahath; and Jahath begat Ahumai, and Lahad. These are the families of the Zorathites” (1 Chronicles 4:2). The Zorathites took their name from Zorah, the town in the lowland from which Samson's father came and from which the Danite spies went out. Ahumai heads a clan rather than a story. The chapter he stands in opens with the great names: “The sons of Judah; Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal” (1 Chronicles 4:1), and runs on through households and sisters — “And these were of the father of Etam; Jezreel, and Ishma, and Idbash: and the name of their sister was Hazelelponi” (1 Chronicles 4:3) — until it stops, without warning, at the one prayer everyone remembers from this chapter: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10). Ahumai is the kind of name among which that prayer is buried, and the burial is instructive: God hears men whose neighbours were only ever names.

corruption_summary: The prayer of Jabez is lifted out of its genealogy and sold as a formula, when its whole force depends on the obscurity of the men around it.
corruption_paragraphs: Jabez's prayer became a bestseller detached from its chapter, and detached it turns into a technique for getting more. In place it is something else: one man among the Ahumais and Lahads and Hazelelponis calls on the God of Israel, and God grants it. The point is not a method but a hearing — that the God of the whole earth attends to a man no one else in history ever mentions again.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God hears obscure men, and that the context of a verse is part of its meaning rather than packaging to be discarded.

pos: n. (the son of Benaiah, serving in his father's monthly course of David's army)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ammizabad, my kinsman has endowed, from 'am, a kinsman or people, and zabad, to bestow or endow; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 27:6.
biblical_def: Ammizabad is named once, as the son serving under his father in the third of David's twelve monthly divisions: “This is that Benaiah, who was mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty: and in his course was Ammizabad his son” (1 Chronicles 27:6). His name means my kinsman has endowed, and the verse itself is an endowment: his whole recorded identity is that he stood in his father's course. Benaiah was the man who killed the lion in the pit in the time of snow and who would one day execute Joab and Shimei at Solomon's word; the Chronicler calls him mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty. To be that man's son and to serve in that man's division is the sum of what Scripture tells us about Ammizabad. The system is laid out at the head of the chapter: “Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:1). Benaiah had the third month (1 Chronicles 27:5); Asahel the brother of Joab had the fourth, “and Zebadiah his son after him” (1 Chronicles 27:7). Sons succeeded fathers in the ranks, and the kingdom was the stronger for it.

corruption_summary: Generational faithfulness is treated as inherited privilege rather than as a trust, though Scripture repeatedly records sons taking their place in their fathers' ranks.
corruption_paragraphs: Ammizabad in his father's course and Zebadiah after Asahel are two instances of the same pattern: a son taking up a post his father held. The modern instinct is to read such a thing as nepotism or as an inheritance to be resented. Scripture records it as order. A father who hands on a trust and a son who takes it up are doing something God repeatedly honours, and the honour belongs to the handing-on as much as to the original exploit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a son who serves faithfully in his father's course is building what his father built, and that Scripture keeps such names on purpose.

pos: n. (a Benjamite, one of the sons of Shashak dwelling in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Antothiyah, probably answers of the LORD, or a man of Anathoth; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 8:24.
biblical_def: Antothijah is named once, in the Chronicler's roll of Benjamin: “And Hananiah, and Elam, and Antothijah” (1 Chronicles 8:24). His name probably means the answers of the LORD, or else marks him a man of Anathoth, the priestly town of Benjamin that would one day produce Jeremiah. The chapter opens the tribe's line formally — “Now Benjamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Aharah the third” (1 Chronicles 8:1) — and then works down through households to the sons of Shashak, of whom Antothijah is one, and on to the next family: “And Iphedeiah, and Penuel, the sons of Shashak” (1 Chronicles 8:25). Then comes the line that explains why the Chronicler troubled to write any of it down: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). This is a register of the men who lived in the holy city — who held households there, who would be there when the city was besieged and burned and who would be remembered when it was rebuilt. Benjamin stayed with Judah when the kingdom divided, and these are the families that stayed.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Jehu in the Simeonite line, named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Asi'el, created of God, from 'asah, to make or do, and 'El, God; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 4:35.
biblical_def: Asiel is named once, four generations back in a Simeonite pedigree: “And Joel, and Jehu the son of Josibiah, the son of Seraiah, the son of Asiel” (1 Chronicles 4:35). His name means created of God, or made by God. The list he belongs to is not idle. The Chronicler is identifying the men who led a particular enterprise, and he says so: “These mentioned by their names were princes in their families: and the house of their fathers increased greatly” (1 Chronicles 4:38). The names around him are as obscure as his own — “And Meshobab, and Jamlech, and Joshah the son of Amaziah” (1 Chronicles 4:34) — and then the chapter tells what these men did: “And these written by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and smote their tents, and the habitations that were found there, and destroyed them utterly unto this day, and dwelt in their rooms: because there was pasture there for their flocks” (1 Chronicles 4:41). A pedigree running back to a man called Created-of-God ends in a company of Simeonites taking pasture for their flocks in the days of a reforming king. Scripture keeps the ancestry because the ancestry is the title.

corruption_paragraphs: The Chronicler lists Asiel because the men who went out in Hezekiah's day were princes in their families and their claim rested on who they were. He is not indulging antiquarian interest; he is establishing title. A people with no memory of where they came from will have no ground to stand on when they are asked by what right they hold anything.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a name meaning created of God confesses the doctrine of creation every time it is spoken, and that the covenant comes to men in families.

pos: n. (a prince of Judah sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the law in the cities of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Ben Chayil, son of strength or son of valour, from ben, a son, and chayil, strength, might or an army; named once in Scripture, at 2 Chronicles 17:7.
biblical_def: Ben-hail is named once, and the thing he was sent to do is one of the most remarkable royal commissions in the Old Testament: “Also in the third year of his reign he sent to his princes, even to Benhail, and to Obadiah, and to Zechariah, and to Nethaneel, and to Michaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah” (2 Chronicles 17:7). His name means son of valour, and his valour was spent on a teaching circuit. Jehoshaphat did not send his princes to collect taxes or to muster troops; he sent them to catechise the nation, and the Chronicler records exactly what they carried: “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people” (2 Chronicles 17:9). Not their own opinions — the book. The king himself is commended for the same reason: “And the LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the first ways of his father David, and sought not unto Baalim” (2 Chronicles 17:3). And the result was national security of a kind no army purchases: “And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were round about Judah, so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat” (2 Chronicles 17:10). A nation taught the law of God was a nation nobody wanted to fight.

corruption_summary: Civil authority is thought to have no business with the law of God, where Jehoshaphat's reform consisted precisely in sending his princes out to teach it.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern settlement treats the magistrate's sphere and God's law as strangers, and treats any contact between them as a threat. 2 Chronicles 17 records a king whose first great act was to send his civil officers through the country with the book of the law to teach the people, and the Holy Ghost commends him for it. The dictionary holds the classical two-kingdoms position — distinct spheres, one Lord over both — and rejects the Radical Two-Kingdoms claim that the magistrate owes God's law no public regard.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the princes carried the book and taught from the book, and that the peace of the land followed the teaching rather than the army.

pos: n. (a Levite of the sons of Merari in the house of Jaaziah, named twice)
etymology: Hebrew Beno, which is simply the Hebrew for “his son”; named at 1 Chronicles 24:26 and 24:27, where the Authorized Version treats it as a proper name.
biblical_def: Beno occurs twice, in two consecutive verses of the register of the priestly and Levitical courses: “The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi: the sons of Jaaziah; Beno” (1 Chronicles 24:26), and “The sons of Merari by Jaaziah; Beno, and Shoham, and Zaccur, and Ibri” (1 Chronicles 24:27). The form is the ordinary Hebrew for his son, and the translators of the Authorized Version took it as the man's name, which is how it stands in the English text. The chapter is the organisation of the priesthood, and it begins at the beginning: “Now these are the divisions of the sons of Aaron. The sons of Aaron; Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar” (1 Chronicles 24:1) — two of whom had been struck dead for offering strange fire. The courses were then assigned by lot, under witness: “These likewise cast lots over against their brethren the sons of Aaron in the presence of David the king, and Zadok, and Ahimelech, and the chief of the fathers of the priests and Levites” (1 Chronicles 24:31). No man chose his own turn at the altar. The lot removed ambition from the service of God, and the Levites of the house of Jaaziah took their order with the rest.

corruption_summary: Office in the church is sought and distributed by ambition and influence, where 1 Chronicles 24 assigns it by lot before witnesses.
corruption_paragraphs: The courses of the priesthood were set by lot in the presence of the king, the high priests, and the chief fathers. The arrangement made it impossible for a family to campaign for the better weeks. Scripture does not make the lot a standing rule for church office — the New Testament gives qualifications and a congregational process instead — but the instinct behind it stands: the service of God is not a career ladder, and a man who manoeuvres for place has already disqualified the motive.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the sons of Aaron included Nadab and Abihu, and that the register which organises worship opens by naming two men who died for presuming in it.
